title: DNA and RNA structure
blurb: Describe the structure of DNA and RNA, apply the base-pairing rules and Chargaff's percentages, and name the three kinds of RNA.
question: A lab report states that a sample of double-stranded DNA is 30% adenine. What percentage is thymine, guanine and cytosine, and why does that rule not apply to a single strand of RNA?

teach.body: Formal definition: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a double helix of two antiparallel strands (one runs 5' to 3', the other 3' to 5') built from nucleotides; it stores an organism's genetic information. Watson and Crick described it in 1953, using Rosalind Franklin's X-ray images. Plain English: DNA is a twisted ladder. The sides are sugar and phosphate; each rung is a pair of bases, and the order of bases spells out the genetic instructions.

head: Part
In DNA
In RNA
teach.caption: The sugar-phosphate backbone is held by covalent phosphodiester bonds; the bases pair across the middle by hydrogen bonds.

teach.body: Bases pair in only two ways: A with T (2 hydrogen bonds) and G with C (3 hydrogen bonds). So in double-stranded DNA, %A = %T and %G = %C. Worked example: if A = 30%, then T = 30%; that leaves 40% for G and C together, so G = 20% and C = 20%. A purine (double ring: adenine, guanine) always pairs with a pyrimidine (single ring: cytosine, thymine, uracil), which keeps the ladder the same width.

items.label: adenine pairs with thymine: 2 hydrogen bonds
guanine pairs with cytosine: 3 hydrogen bonds
A/T/G/C if a sample is 30% adenine

teach.caption: Memory hook: "Pure As Gold" = PURines are Adenine and Guanine.
A gene is a segment of DNA that codes for a protein (or a functional RNA). The genome is all of an organism's DNA.

rows.label: Location
values: Made in nucleus; works in cytoplasm too

teach.caption: In RNA, uracil (U) replaces thymine and pairs with adenine.

head: RNA
Full name
Job
rows: Carries the code as codons to the ribosome
Brings a specific amino acid; has the anticodon
Structural and catalytic part of ribosomes

teach.h: Worked scenario: Priya checks a lab report
teach.body: Priya, a nursing applicant working as a lab aide, reads that a double-stranded DNA sample has 1,000 bases, 220 of them guanine. Because G pairs with C, cytosine is also 220. That uses 440 bases, leaving 560 for A and T, which must be equal: 280 adenine and 280 thymine. If the sample were single-stranded RNA, she could not use this shortcut: with no partner strand, A need not equal U and G need not equal C.

teach.text: Common traps: RNA has URACIL and DNA has THYMINE (not the reverse); pairs are A-T and G-C, never A-G or C-T; the backbone is held by covalent bonds and only the base pairs use hydrogen bonds; if A = 30%, G is 20%, not 30%; tRNA carries the ANTIcodon, mRNA carries the codons.

items: DNA: double helix, antiparallel strands; nucleotide = phosphate + deoxyribose + base.
A-T (2 H-bonds), G-C (3 H-bonds); in DNA %A = %T and %G = %C.
Purines (A, G) double ring; pyrimidines (C, T, U) single ring.
DNA wraps around histones: nucleosomes, chromatin, chromosomes.
RNA: single-stranded, ribose, uracil. mRNA codons, tRNA anticodon + amino acid, rRNA in ribosomes.

summary: You can now describe a nucleotide, the double helix and how DNA is packaged, apply the A-T and G-C pairing rules to work out base percentages, and contrast DNA with RNA. You can also state the job of mRNA, tRNA and rRNA.

A.q: In a double-stranded DNA molecule, which base pairs with thymine?
A.why: Adenine pairs with thymine through 2 hydrogen bonds.

whyNot.0: Guanine pairs with cytosine, not thymine.
whyNot.2: Cytosine pairs with guanine; two pyrimidines never pair together.
whyNot.3: Uracil is found in RNA, not DNA, and it pairs with adenine.

A.q: A sample of double-stranded DNA is 30% adenine. What percentage of its bases are guanine?
A.why: A = T = 30%, so A + T = 60%. The remaining 40% is split equally between G and C, so G = 20%.

whyNot.1: 30% is the thymine value (T = A); guanine matches cytosine, not adenine.
whyNot.2: 40% is G and C combined; guanine is half of that.
whyNot.3: 70% is everything except adenine, not the guanine share.

A.q: Which sugar is found in the nucleotides of RNA?
A.why: RNA (ribonucleic acid) contains ribose; DNA contains deoxyribose.

whyNot.0: Deoxyribose is the sugar in DNA.
whyNot.1: Glucose is a 6-carbon fuel sugar, not a nucleotide sugar.
whyNot.3: Fructose is a 6-carbon sugar found in fruit and sucrose, not in nucleic acids.

B.q: Which molecule carries an anticodon and delivers a specific amino acid to the ribosome?
B.why: tRNA has an anticodon that pairs with an mRNA codon, and it carries the matching amino acid.

whyNot.0: mRNA carries the codons that the anticodons pair with.
whyNot.1: rRNA forms the structure and catalytic core of the ribosome; it does not ferry amino acids.
whyNot.2: DNA polymerase is an enzyme that builds new DNA during replication.

B.q: What holds the two strands of a DNA double helix together?
options: Peptide bonds between the base pairs
Ionic bonds between the two sugars
B.why: Complementary bases on opposite strands are joined by hydrogen bonds (2 for A-T, 3 for G-C).

whyNot.1: Peptide bonds join amino acids in proteins, not DNA bases.
whyNot.2: Covalent (phosphodiester) bonds hold each strand's backbone, not the pairs across the middle.
whyNot.3: The sugars are in the backbones on the outside and are not bonded across to each other.

B.q: Which statement about DNA bases is correct?
options: Adenine and guanine are single-ring bases
A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine
Two purines pair across the helix
B.why: Each pair is one purine (double ring) plus one pyrimidine (single ring), keeping the helix a constant width.

whyNot.0: Adenine and guanine are purines, which have a double ring.
whyNot.2: Cytosine and thymine are pyrimidines, which have a single ring.
whyNot.3: Two purines would be too wide; a purine always pairs with a pyrimidine.

C.q: A double-stranded DNA segment contains 200 bases, 60 of which are cytosine. How many of its bases are adenine?
C.why: C = 60, so G = 60, giving 120. That leaves 200 - 120 = 80 for A + T, and A = T, so A = 40.

whyNot.0: 60 is the guanine count (G = C), not adenine.
whyNot.1: 70 comes from (200 - 60) / 2, which forgets that guanine also equals 60.
whyNot.3: 80 is adenine and thymine combined; adenine is half of that.

C.q: Which comparison of DNA and RNA is correct?
options: DNA has uracil; RNA has thymine instead
DNA has ribose; RNA has deoxyribose
DNA leaves the nucleus; RNA stays inside
DNA is double; RNA is usually single
C.why: DNA is a double-stranded helix; RNA is usually a single strand.

whyNot.0: Reversed: DNA has thymine and RNA has uracil.
whyNot.1: Reversed: DNA has deoxyribose and RNA has ribose.
whyNot.2: Reversed: DNA stays in the nucleus, while RNA such as mRNA travels to the cytoplasm.

C.q: One strand of DNA reads 5'-ATGCCA-3'. What is the complementary strand, written 3' to 5'?
C.why: Pair each base (A-T, T-A, G-C, C-G) in order: ATGCCA pairs with TACGGT, running 3' to 5' because the strands are antiparallel.

whyNot.1: Uracil belongs in RNA; a complementary DNA strand uses thymine.
whyNot.2: TGGCAT is the complement written 5' to 3'; labeling it 3' to 5' reverses the order and ignores that the strands are antiparallel.
whyNot.3: This pairs A with G and T with C, which breaks the A-T and G-C rules.

reteach.title: A zipper with two kinds of teeth
reteach.question: Picture a zipper where the teeth come in matching shapes: a short tooth always meets a long tooth. How does that describe DNA?

blocks.body: The two fabric strips are the sugar-phosphate backbones, sewn tight (covalent bonds). The teeth are the bases. A long tooth (a purine) always locks with a short tooth (a pyrimidine), so the zipper stays an even width. The A tooth only fits the T tooth with 2 hooks; the G tooth fits the C tooth with 3 hooks, which makes G-C a slightly stronger grip. The hooks are hydrogen bonds: easy to unzip when the cell needs to read or copy the code.

blocks.text: RNA is half a zipper: one strip, and its A teeth pair with U, not T.

explain.body: Each nucleotide is a phosphate + a 5-carbon sugar (deoxyribose in DNA) + a nitrogenous base. Sugars and phosphates link by covalent phosphodiester bonds to form each strand's backbone.

test.q: A single DNA nucleotide is made of:
options: Phosphate, ribose sugar and a base
test.why: A DNA nucleotide is a phosphate group, the sugar deoxyribose and one nitrogenous base.

whyNot.0: Ribose is the sugar in RNA nucleotides, not DNA.
whyNot.2: Amino acids are the monomers of proteins, not part of nucleotides.
whyNot.3: Glycerol is part of fats and phospholipids, not nucleotides.

explain.body: A pairs with T by 2 hydrogen bonds; G pairs with C by 3. In double-stranded DNA, %A = %T and %G = %C, so knowing one base gives you all four.

test.q: How many hydrogen bonds join a guanine-cytosine base pair?
test.why: G-C pairs are held by 3 hydrogen bonds; A-T pairs by 2.

whyNot.0: 2 hydrogen bonds join an A-T pair, not G-C.
whyNot.1: No DNA base pair is held by a single hydrogen bond.
whyNot.3: 4 overstates it; G-C pairs have 3 hydrogen bonds.

explain.body: In eukaryotes DNA wraps around histone proteins to form nucleosomes, which coil into chromatin and condense into chromosomes. A gene is a DNA segment that codes for a protein or functional RNA.

test.q: In eukaryotic cells, DNA wraps around proteins called ______ to form nucleosomes.
test.why: Histones are the spool proteins that DNA winds around to form nucleosomes.

whyNot.0: Ribosomes make proteins; DNA does not wrap around them.
whyNot.1: A centromere is the region joining sister chromatids, not a spool protein.
whyNot.2: Chromatids are the copies of a replicated chromosome, not the proteins DNA wraps around.

explain.body: RNA is usually single-stranded, uses ribose and has uracil instead of thymine. mRNA carries codons from the nucleus to the ribosome; tRNA brings amino acids and has the anticodon; rRNA builds the ribosome.

test.q: Which type of RNA forms the structural and catalytic core of ribosomes?
test.why: Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) is the structural and catalytic part of the ribosome.

whyNot.1: mRNA carries the coded message to the ribosome; it is read, not built into it.
whyNot.2: tRNA delivers amino acids to the ribosome.
whyNot.3: Pre-mRNA is the unprocessed transcript that becomes mRNA.
